name: Momin Khan Momin
bio: Momin of Delhi is described in the book as the author of six long masnawis, skilled in medicine, astronomy and astrology, and deeply read in poetry. He is said at first to have lived a gay and reckless life, and in old age to have given himself to prayer and fasting, acquiring great contemporary fame; his work is called the most delicate flower of Urdu expression.

The one piece given here is drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. It is a free rendering, not a literal translation, and the original Urdu poem is untitled; it is named here by its first line.

poems.title: Wherever the Beloved looks she stirs
poems.author: Momin Khan Momin
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
Wherever the Beloved looks she stirs
    Trouble and longing sore and eager breath
And deep desire in all her worshippers,
    And some for her have drunk the cup of Death.

O Night of Separation, darkest night
    Of deepest grief, thy cruelty shall cease;
To-morrow I shall greet the dawning light
    Within the city of Eternal Peace.

O threatening Whirlwind rolling on thy way,
    I shall unloose thy knot, if thou but dare
With angry gusts to toss and disarray
    A single curl of the Beloved's hair.

Sometimes her beauty goads and maddens me,
    I cannot bear her cruel loveliness,
But turn her mirror that she may not see;
    Why should I let her double my distress?

Hearken, O Momin, all thy life is done!
    In idol-worship at the Temple thou
Hast spent thy days, and thus thy years have run:
    How canst thou call thyself a Muslim now?
